outputs.L1:
**How Do I Love Thee? (Sonnet 43)**

How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.  
I love thee to the depth and breadth and height  
My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight  
For the ends of Being and ideal Grace.  
I love thee to the level of every day’s  
Most quiet need, by sun and candlelight.  
I love thee freely, as men strive for Right;  
I love thee purely, as they turn from Praise.  
I love thee with the passion put to use  
In my old griefs, and with my childhood’s faith.  
I love thee with a love I seemed to lose  
With my lost saints. I love thee with the breath,  
Smiles, tears, of all my life; and, if God choose,  
I shall but love thee better after death.

**Poetry Out Loud Note:** In the print anthology, this poem is titled simply “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.” During the recitation, the student may use either title.
outputs.L2:
In how many forms does my love for you exist? I will name them. My spirit loves you as far as it can extend in every direction—even beyond what can be seen—as it reaches toward life’s ultimate purpose and perfect grace. I love you with the same steadiness as the simplest daily necessities, both in daylight and by candlelight. My love is given willingly, like the efforts of those who pursue justice, and without selfish motives, like people who do good without seeking admiration. I love you with the intensity once devoted to past sorrows and with the unquestioning trust I possessed as a child. I love you with the devotion I thought had disappeared when I lost the saints I once revered. Every breath, joy, and tear throughout my life expresses my love for you; and, if God permits, that love will become even greater after I die.

**Poetry Out Loud note:** In the printed anthology, the work is titled only “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.” During the recitation, the student may use either title.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s love is vast and all-encompassing, reaching the deepest, widest, and highest limits of the soul. It is present not only in the pursuit of spiritual ideals but also in the ordinary needs and routines of everyday life. This love is given freely, without obligation, and purely, without any desire for praise or recognition.

The speaker’s feelings are strengthened by the full range of past experience. The passion once connected to grief, the unquestioning faith of childhood, and the devotion once given to lost beliefs have all been transformed into love for the beloved. Ultimately, the speaker loves with every breath, smile, and tear—with every part of life—and expresses the hope that, by God’s grace, this love will become even greater after death.
outputs.L4: The speaker begins by asking how deeply and in how many ways she loves her beloved, then sets out to measure that love. She describes it as vast and spiritual, reaching to the furthest depths and heights her soul can imagine. At the same time, her love appears in the ordinary needs and actions of everyday life, freely and naturally given. It is also morally pure: she loves without selfishness, with the sincerity of those who seek what is right and the humility of those who avoid praise. Her devotion carries the intensity once attached to past sorrows and childhood faith, while also embracing her smiles, tears, breath, and entire life. Ultimately, she declares that her love involves every part of her being and will endure throughout her lifetime. Trusting in divine grace, she even hopes that after death she will love her beloved more strongly still.
